name: Battle of Drepana
intro: Off Drepana (Trapani), western Sicily, 249 BC. You are the consul Publius Claudius Pulcher, with about 120 ships, hoping to surprise the Carthaginian fleet of Adherbal in its harbour.
debrief: In Polybius’s account, Claudius sailed by night, but his fleet arrived strung out. Adherbal led his ships out of the harbour by another channel to open water. As the Roman ships turned back, they collided and ended up with their sterns to the shore, where Adherbal’s better crews rammed them; 93 Roman ships were taken. Claudius escaped with about thirty. Later writers tell how he had the sacred chickens thrown overboard, saying ‘let them drink, since they will not eat’. He was tried at Rome and fined. The other choices are what-ifs.

win: The Roman line holds at sea.
lose: The Roman ships are pinned to the shore.

decisions.title: A night sailing
decisions.text: You are the consul Publius Claudius Pulcher, commanding the fleet off Lilybaeum. You plan to surprise the Carthaginian fleet in its harbour at Drepana by sailing through the night.

hint.text: Your crews are tired and new.

scout.text: Surprise works only if you arrive in order and on time.

choices.label: Sail by night to surprise them at dawn

fx.text: The fleet sails at midnight, strung out in the dark.

choices.label: Sail by day in close order

fx.text: The fleet sails in good order, but will be seen coming.

choices.label: Blockade Drepana and wait for them to come out

decisions.title: The sacred chickens
decisions.text: Before battle, the sacred chickens must eat. The keeper reports they will not touch the grain.

scout.text: A bad omen ignored loudly will frighten the men more than any enemy.

choices.label: ‘If they will not eat, let them drink!’ Throw them over

fx.text: You throw the chickens into the sea. The crews are horrified.

choices.label: Wait a day for better omens

fx.text: The fleet waits. The crews are calm.

choices.label: Quietly find a keeper who sees good signs

fx.text: A new keeper reports the birds are eating.

decisions.title: Adherbal comes out
decisions.text: At dawn your leading ships reach the harbour mouth. Adherbal sees you and leads his fleet out by the other side, round the island, to the open sea.

hint.text: Your ships are strung out along the coast, and the harbour is a trap.

scout.text: Pull your leading ships out of the harbour and form a line before he attacks.

choices.label: Turn the fleet round and form along the shore

fx.text: The ships in front turn back into those behind. Oars break; the fleet ends up with its sterns to the shore.

choices.label: Form a line out at sea and meet him there

fx.text: Your well-ordered fleet forms a line in open water and meets Adherbal ship for ship.

choices.label: Push on into the harbour and attack the port

fx.text: Your ships crowd into the empty harbour.

decisions.title: Pinned against the shore
decisions.text: Adherbal attacks. Your ships have the shore behind them and no room to move.

hint.text: Your ships cannot back water: the shore is behind them.

scout.text: Break out to sea where you can, before you are rammed one by one.

fx.text: Ship after ship is rammed and cannot escape. The Carthaginians have sea room; you have none.

choices.label: Break out to sea at one end of the line

fx.text: Some ships break out and fight in open water.

choices.label: Abandon the ships and save the crews ashore

fx.text: The ships are lost, but many men live.

decisions.title: Escape
decisions.text: The battle is lost. Your flagship is near the end of the line.

hint.text: There is a gap at the southern end.

scout.text: Lead what ships you can out.

choices.label: Lead the survivors out through the gap

fx.text: You escape with about thirty ships. Ninety-three are taken.

choices.label: Stay and fight to the last ship

fx.text: The last ships are taken around you.

choices.label: Beach the ships and march to Lilybaeum

fx.text: The crews fight their way to Lilybaeum overland.

quotes.text: Let them drink, since they will not eat!
quotes.who: Claudius Pulcher, throwing the sacred chickens into the sea, as later writers tell it
